extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in humor, laughter, and gelotology
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes scientific, philosophical, physiological, and social criteria about laughter and its causes, structure, functions, and therapeutic uses—useful for understanding how and why humor elicits laughter and how laughter operates in interaction. Relevant for creators, performers, therapists, and researchers who need principles for producing or evaluating humorous material and laughter-based interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness (clarity of incongruity resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the basic laws of a comedian: 'when the audience is confused, it doesn't laugh' (referred to as 'exactness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke must create an inconsistency that the audience can resolve; confusion prevents laughter. Anti-pattern: leaving the audience puzzled about the joke's point or punchline. Example note from the page: 'Sometimes the inconsistency may be resolved and there may still be no laugh'—so exactness is necessary but not always sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity–resolution / Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke creates an inconsistency (incongruity) and the audience tries to understand it; if they solve this 'cognitive riddle' and realize the surprise was not dangerous, they 'laugh with relief'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft humor so an unexpected element is introduced and then resolved in a way that removes perceived threat/tension. This is the justification for using laughter as a coping mechanism. Anti-pattern: unresolved incongruity (no laugh) or a resolution that restores a sense of danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and rhythm of delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the incongruity (and aspects of its timing and rhythm) affects how hard or long the audience laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to pacing, beats, and rhythmic placement of the punchline; small timing adjustments can change laugh strength and duration. Consider interplay of micro-timing (pauses, syllable stress) and larger rhythmic patterns in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential organization and placement in interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is sequentially organized and precisely placed relative to surrounding talk; overlapped laughter is often timed relative to the partner's laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In conversational or improvised comedy, place laughter (and prompts for audience laughter) in relation to turns, responses, and partner actions. Use overlap strategically; misplaced or ill-timed laughter can undermine the comic effect or social coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social signaling and group-cohesion function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is used as a signal for being part of a group—it signals acceptance and positive interactions with others and can be contagious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use laughter to build rapport and signal inclusion; in performance, foster shared frames so audience laughter becomes contagious. Be aware that social context (age, gender, culture) affects whether laughter will be elicited or considered appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory (comparative humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's view: 'The passion of laughter is nothing else but sudden glory arising from sudden conception of some eminency in ourselves, by comparison with the infirmity of others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor that invites a benign comparison (us vs. them or self vs. past self) can elicit laughter via feelings of superiority; guard against mean-spiritedness that creates social harm. Consider audience sensitivities and ethical boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bellieni three-step process (oddness → resolution → release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bellieni's model: (1) a situation that seems odd and induces incongruity, (2) the worry/stress provoked must be worked out and overcome (resolution), (3) the release of laughter acts as an 'all-clear' signal to bystanders (relief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-step model when structuring material: create an oddity, ensure a perceivable cognitive or emotional resolution, then allow/trigger release. This is a practical framework for crafting jokes and comic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity vs 'sham mirth'
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between genuine mirth and 'sham mirth' (unpleasant or pathological laughter where the person appears to be laughing but reports undesirable sensations at the punch line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance, strive for eliciting authentic mirth; in therapeutic or clinical contexts, distinguish between genuine laughter and pathological or socially forced laughter. Anti-pattern: eliciting awkward or forced 'courtesy' laughs that undermine trust or wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic and phonetic structure of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughs commonly consist of sequences of bursts (e.g., 'ha-ha-ha'), often with higher pitch than speech; there are constraints on which note sequences occur, and phonetic/prosodic details coordinate interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For performers and researchers, consider prosody, burst patterns, pitch, and inter-note intervals when analyzing or staging laughter. Use natural laugh patterns; avoid physiologically unnatural sequences (e.g., 'ha-ho-ha-ho' is physically unnatural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and physiological plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every imaginable laugh occurs; some laugh structures are physically impossible due to vocal-cord limitations. Normal note durations and inter-note intervals follow physiological constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design laugh cues and imitations to conform to natural vocal patterns. Artificial or exaggerated laugh forms that violate physiological norms risk sounding inauthentic or awkward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as interactional management (managing delicate or serious moments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Far more than merely a response to humor, laughter often works to manage delicate and serious moments and helps accomplish actions and regulate relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use laughter strategically in dialogue and performance to defuse tension, signal shifts in stance, or reframe seriousness. Be mindful that laughter can also inappropriately deflect or minimize serious concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic application caveats and training needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter therapy has reported benefits (stress reduction, immune effects, improved quality of life in some studies) but evidence is limited; caregivers need training to use humor effectively and well-designed randomized trials are lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying laughter therapeutically, combine it with other treatments, obtain appropriate training, and be cautious about claims of efficacy; monitor for limited harmful side effects and tailor approaches to patient needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative and harmful functions of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is not always positive: excessive laughter can be pathological (cataplexy, fits), and laughter can express scorn, schadenfreude, or be used as a social corrective (Bergson) that can stigmatize or punish eccentric behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comedic material for potential to harm, ostracize, or stigmatize. Avoid humor that relies on humiliating targets or reinforcing damaging social norms; consider ethical implications and audience vulnerability.
